title: Interactive profiling sandbox: samplerless microtraces and perf-snapshot recipes
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a lightweight, interactive sandbox for investigating token-path latency regressions and transient stalls without standing up the full sampler pipeline. The idea is to quickly iterate on hypotheses (scheduler preemption, GPU kernel stalls, kvcache miss storms, serialization hotspots) by collecting short 'microtraces' tied to synthetic requests and then folding them into a compact perf-snapshot that can be visualized as flamegraphs or a small trace timeline.

Design principles (why this exists):
- fast feedback: get a usable flame/timeline within 30–90s from a repro run
- low infrastructure churn: no long-lived eBPF collector, no heavyweight tracing agent for the first-pass
- reproducible artifacts: produce a tarball with the perf.data, user-space stack maps, and a short manifest for CI attachment
- easy to escalate: artifacts should include the minimal hints to decide whether to run a heavier full-run with the production sampler.

When to use this sandbox:
- intermittent latency spikes during stress test runs
- PRs that add new lock paths or introduce extra context switches
- GPU memory allocation stalls suspected but not confirmed
- quick triage on a CI failure before asking SRE to run the golden sampler

Quickstart (local dev machine or a dedicated perf node)
1) spin up a small reproducer that exercises the slow path (example: model load + 1-2 long tokens)
2) start the subject process as root or with CAP_SYS_ADMIN so perf can attach
3) run the microtrace helper: ./bin/microtrace.sh --samples 6 --duration 12s --out ./snapshots/run-$(date +%s).tar.gz

microtrace.sh (high-level behaviour)
- for i in 1..samples:
    - sleep jitter(0..15s) to avoid hitting the same scheduler window repeatedly
    - run perf record -F 997 -g --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> -o perf.data.tmp -- sleep <duration>
    - collect /proc/<pid>/stack and /proc/<pid>/status for context
    - if user-space symbols are stripped, run nm/map-scripts to harvest symbol maps
    - fold perf.data.tmp into a named perf.data for that sample
- build a manifest.json with command, kernel, glibc, driver versions and round metadata
- tar.gz the perf.data files, manifest, and small wrapper that can produce flamegraphs

Notes on sampling frequency and why 997 Hz
- We need a high enough sampling rate to expose short CPU bursts that cause token stalls but not so high it overwhelms the node or skews scheduling. 997 is a pragmatic default (prime helps spread alignments).
- If the node is already under heavy load, drop to 200–500 and favor longer sample durations (20–40s).

Generating a flamegraph locally
- unpack snapshot -> cd run-XXXXXXXX
- for each perf.data: sudo perf script -i perf.data | ./scripts/stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.folded
- cat *.folded | ./scripts/flamegraph.pl --title="microtrace run" > microtrace.svg

Samplers vs samplerless: heuristics for escalation
- samplerless wins: short-lived spikes correlated with a small number of threads, quick reproductions, or when we only need a flame to see a new call-site.
- run the full sampler when: we see cross-host variance, drive-level I/O stalls, or need full KV cache KVS events that require the production eBPF maps or the long-run prefix cache aggregation.

Common patterns and how to interpret them
- many tiny stacks attributed to futex_wait or nanosleep -> look for lock contention in user code and thread pool starvation
- single hot user function with long wall time but low CPU -> likely a blocking syscall (fsync, open) or GPU wait; cross-check with iostat and nvidia-smi timestamps
- intermittent spikes with kernel 'preempt' frames near wakeup -> scheduler preemption caused by misconfigured cgroups or aggressive background cron jobs
- sudden growth in 'brk/mmap' frames -> check custom allocators and arena growth (asan/je debug builds can help)

Lightweight timeline extraction (cheap alternative to full traces)
- we capture sample timestamps and attach them to a 1–5s resolution timeline: sample N -> timestamp T -> approximate event at T +/- 5ms. Not as precise as full traces but good enough to correlate with external metrics (GPU load, network buffers, host-level spikes).

CI perf-job snippet (for quick guardrail)
- job: perf-microtrace-check
  stage: perf
  image: ubuntu:22.04
  script:
    - apt-get update && apt-get install -y linux-tools-common linux-tools-generic perf
    - ./bin/microtrace.sh --samples 3 --duration 10 --out artifacts/perf-microtrace-$(CI_PIPELINE_ID).tar.gz
    - upload-artifact artifacts/*.tar.gz
  timeout: 30m

This CI job is intentionally short to keep runtime and cost bounded. Attach the tarball to the pipeline for on-demand debugging.

Known limitations and gotchas
- perf needs consistent kernel configs and matching vmlinux to get kernel symbolization. Include /proc/kallsyms in the manifest and vmlinux reference when possible.
- On GKE-managed nodes or some distros, perf may be blocked by seccomp or missing CAP_SYS_ADMIN. If we cannot run perf, fallback to strace + /proc/cpuinfo sampling (noisy but sometimes informative).
- GPU stalls are harder: perf captures CPU-side waits but not CUDA kernel stalls. Combine with nvidia-smi --query and the small GPU-monitor snapshot script we keep in /ops/gpu-monitor/

Investigation checklist (starter)
- reproduce locally with small harness (yes/no)
- run microtraces x3 and check for repeated frames (yes/no)
- if repeated: generate flame, identify top 5 callsites, open PR to annotate with profiler labels if needed
- if non-repeated: run a full-day sampler run or ask SRE for golden-trace (link with JIRA)

Next steps and TODOs
- add a small python wrapper to auto-subdivide perf.data by thread and produce per-thread flames (Priya)
- add an option to collect lightweight GPU telemetry in the same snapshot (Marco)
- integrate a 'fast-compare' mode that diffs two snapshots and highlights new callsites (Sofia)

Notes to self:
- keep default sample count small in PR pipelines to avoid flapping. When a developer requests escalation, ask for: a) stable repro, b) two snapshots (good/bad), c) approximate wall-clock window when the spike happened.

References and helper links:
- scripts used: scripts/stackcollapse-perf.pl, scripts/flamegraph.pl (bundled from Brendan Gregg)
- useful debug commands: sudo perf record -F 997 -g -p <pid> -- sleep 12; sudo perf script | head -n 100
- escalation playbook: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/viewpage.action?pageId=48219

End of sandbox notes (versioned, iterative).
